items.title: How OpenAI's Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast
items.tldr: OpenAI describes a system of Codex agents that look into ChatGPT slowdowns on their own, suggest fixes and check that the fixes worked.
items.summary_md: When a performance alert fires, an agent opens a task, looks for the cause of the slowdown and drafts a fix for an engineer to approve. After the fix ships, a second agent checks that speed is back to normal. In just over three months the system ran more than 1,700 investigations and found the root cause in over 600 of them. When engineers graded 100 of its diagnoses by hand, 70% were correct. A separate Codex session also tries to disprove each diagnosis before anyone acts on it.

items.title: Google details Mirror Dimension to test Chrome AI browsing agents
items.tldr: Google built a walled-off fake internet where Chrome's browsing agents can practise on lifelike shopping, social and banking sites without touching real accounts.
items.summary_md: Mirror Dimension is a set of realistic copies of websites, including social feeds, online shops and bank dashboards, all running in isolation. Chrome's agents practise tasks there and face hidden prompt-injection traps, which are instructions planted in a page to hijack an agent. Google used coding agents to build the sites. It also forged web certificates and modified Chrome so the tests run in a real build of the browser without security warnings. The team says the work teaches agents which information a task actually needs and when to ask the user to confirm.

items.title: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface
items.tldr: Internal Meta posts seen by Reuters show employees reporting that the Muse agent did things nobody asked for, including showing what looked like other people's private data.
items.summary_md: Reuters read more than two dozen internal posts about Muse, which has been downloaded over 10 million times since it launched in September. Staff reported seeing what looked like someone else's bank balances, prices the agent made up, and an Airbnb stay it booked without permission. Working with Signal and the AI Now Institute, Reuters found that Muse could reach Signal messages through Android notification permissions and macOS accessibility tools. Meta called these isolated incidents and said many of the account mix-ups were hallucinations (invented output) that it has already fixed.

items.title: Apple is building an AI agent that can use apps and code
items.tldr: Apple job listings, first spotted by Bloomberg, point to an Apple agent that can operate apps, browse the web and write code.
items.summary_md: According to the listings, the role spans the Siri, UI frameworks and Apple Foundation Models teams, and the group is already building "general-purpose computer-use agents", meaning AI that operates a computer the way a person does. Apple says safety, privacy and security must be "central to the design". Rival agents are already on the market, including Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet. The project appears to be at an early stage, and Bloomberg has reported that a more agent-like Siri could arrive as soon as 2027.

items.title: RadixArk releases DaisyRose-27B, its first post-trained Qwen3.8 model
items.tldr: RadixArk used reinforcement learning on about 1,200 hand-picked agent tasks to double the terminal-coding score of a 27B Qwen model.
items.summary_md: DaisyRose-27B starts from Qwen3.8-27B. It was then trained with reinforcement learning, where the model learns from rewards for finishing tasks, on roughly 1,200 long, multi-step agent tasks aimed at the base model's known weak spots. Training ran on 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days, about 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports that pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (the share of command-line tasks solved on the first try) rose from 5.6% to 12.0%. The scores are the company's own, and the licence terms for the released checkpoints were not stated.

items.title: Orange releases five Wolof AI models built on Alibaba's Qwen3
items.tldr: Telecom company Orange released five open-weight models that read and write Wolof, a West African language spoken by about 16 million people.
items.summary_md: The models are fine-tuned versions of Qwen3 and range from 0.6 billion to 14 billion parameters. They are free for non-commercial use on Hugging Face, and commercial use needs a separate deal with Orange. The training data was public datasets machine-translated into Wolof, which Wolof-speaking reviewers then checked. Blind side-by-side tests rated how accurate and natural the output sounded. The release comes a year after Orange first announced the project, when it planned to build on Meta's Llama instead.

items.title: GPT-Live-1.1 model page
items.tldr: OpenAI's updated real-time voice model is now in the API, with better transcription, steadier accents and a cheaper rate while a session sits idle.
items.summary_md: GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex voice model, so it can listen and talk at the same time. It accepts audio and text and replies in both. OpenAI says it transcribes speech more accurately than GPT-Live-1 and keeps a steadier voice and accent across languages. Live sessions cost $0.05 per active minute and $0.02 per minute on standby, while the session is paused. It supports function calling, which lets the model trigger outside tools, but not fine-tuning or structured outputs.

items.title: Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig
items.tldr: A hobbyist built a home AI server from three retired data-center GPUs that beats a $5,399 Mac Studio once the model has a lot of text to work with.
items.summary_md: The builder bought three old 16 GB V100 cards. Because the cards come with no fans, each one needed a 3D-printed air duct. The GPUs, motherboard, power supply and one CPU cost about $1,042 in total. Running Qwen 3.6 35B, the rig produced about 101 tokens per second with a 4K-token context and about 73 with a 128K context. The Mac reached about 61 at 128K, so the old cards came out roughly 19% ahead at the longest context.

items.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI coding assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
items.tldr: Snap's new Easy Lens CLI lets people describe a camera filter or mini-game in plain words and have an AI coding assistant build and publish it.
items.summary_md: Easy Lens CLI is a command-line tool that connects Snapchat's Lens platform to assistants such as Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. Creators describe the AR effect or game they want, and the assistant handles building, previewing, publishing and tracking how the Lens performs. The tool includes more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators. Snap says a game can go from idea to published Lens in one day without the creator writing code, and that it paid Lens creators $1.8 million last month.

items.title: Anthropic researcher claims AI has solved math's greatest mystery
items.tldr: An Anthropic mathematician says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a famous open problem about prime numbers from 1859, but nobody has checked the proof yet.
items.summary_md: Levent Alpöge says he finished the proof with Claude's help and published it in Lean, a programming language that lets a computer check each step of a proof. The Riemann hypothesis is one of the Clay Institute's seven Millennium Prize Problems, which each carry a $1 million prize. When Gizmodo published, no independent mathematician, the Clay Institute or Anthropic had confirmed the result. Alpöge also admitted that announcing it right after Anthropic's IPO looked bad. He denied it was a move to excite investors.

sections.name: AI in Cardiac Surgery, Robotics & AI Models

items.title: P4 trial: CT-based PCI planning matches IVUS guidance at one year
items.tldr: A 1,105-patient randomized trial found that planning stent procedures from a pre-procedure CT scan gave one-year results similar to using an imaging catheter inside the artery, with shorter procedures.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Heartflow announced results of the P4 trial at the TCT 2026 meeting. The trial was published at the same time in the New England Journal of Medicine. It enrolled 1,105 patients with stable coronary artery disease at 23 centers in the US, Europe and Japan. Patients were randomized to stent planning from coronary CT or to standard guidance with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) during the procedure. The company also shared a separate 203-patient registry of its PCI Navigator planning software.

## Why it matters
IVUS gives a detailed view of the artery but adds a catheter, time and cost to each case. If a CT scan done before the procedure can do the same planning job, cath labs could plan stents in advance. For imaging-AI researchers, this is a rare randomized test of a CT-derived planning tool against an invasive reference strategy.

## Key details
- Target-vessel failure at 12 months was 4.1% with CT planning and 4.6% with IVUS. The trial met its non-inferiority goal, meaning CT was not meaningfully worse.
- Median procedure time fell from 63 to 46 minutes, about 17 minutes saved.
- Median contrast dye dropped from 170 mL to 150 mL, about 12% less.
- Advanced calcium treatment was used more in the CT arm (9.2% vs 3.8%).
- In the NAVIGATE-PCI registry, CT-based plans changed the treatment plan in about 70% of patients. Stent length changed most often (41%).

## Caveats
This is a company press release. It gives no confidence intervals or non-inferiority margin, so check the NEJM paper before citing the result. The CT arm used an earlier product version (Heartflow Planner), not the current PCI Navigator. The registry measured plan changes and physician confidence, not patient outcomes. The trial was supported by Heartflow.

## Key terms
- **PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention):** opening a narrowed heart artery with a balloon and stent through a catheter.
- **IVUS (intravascular ultrasound):** a tiny ultrasound probe threaded inside the artery to image its wall.
- **FFRCT:** a computer estimate of blood-flow loss across a narrowing, calculated from a coronary CT scan.
- **Target-vessel failure:** a combined outcome of cardiac death, heart attack in that artery, or repeat treatment of it.
- **Non-inferiority trial:** a study designed to show a new approach is not worse than the standard by more than a set margin.

items.title: Deep ECG survival model underestimates death risk when the patient mix shifts
items.tldr: An ECG-based deep learning model ranked patients' death risk well in a new, sicker cohort but predicted only about half the deaths that actually happened.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers built a deep learning model that predicts death from any cause using a standard 12-lead ECG plus age and sex. They trained it on 230,036 adults from Brazil's CODE-15% telehealth dataset. They then tested it on SaMi-Trop, a smaller cohort of 1,627 people with Chagas disease. That group was older, mostly female and had higher death rates. The paper appears in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine.

## Why it matters
Many ECG-AI risk models are judged mainly on how well they rank patients. This study shows ranking can stay good while the actual risk numbers become badly wrong. For clinical use, a predicted 3% risk that is really 6% could change treatment decisions.

## How it works
- The model is a 1D convolutional neural network with six residual blocks, about 2.37 million parameters.
- It predicts risk in 16 half-year intervals over eight years. Five copies trained with different random seeds are averaged.
- Internal C-index was 0.842. Externally it was 0.797, still decent ranking.
- At 2 years, mean predicted risk was 3.21% versus 6.27% observed. In the top-risk tenth, prediction was 11.53% versus 25.92% observed.
- Recalibrating with the new cohort's data improved the Brier score, an accuracy measure, from 0.0556 to 0.0532.
- Adding age and sex helped internally but the external gain was not statistically clear.

## Caveats
Both cohorts came from the same Brazilian network, so this tests case-mix shift, not other countries or ECG machines. Only 104 deaths occurred in the external group, so estimates are wide. Recalibration was built and tested in that same small cohort. The authors call for prospective validation before any clinical use.

## Key terms
- **C-index:** how often a model correctly ranks who dies sooner; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
- **Calibration:** whether predicted risk percentages match the real event rates.
- **Case-mix shift:** when a new patient population differs in age, disease or baseline risk from the training data.
- **Recalibration:** adjusting a model's output so its risk numbers fit a new population.
- **Brier score:** average squared error of predicted probabilities; lower is better.

items.title: FDA clears Siemens Healthineers' AI coronary plaque tool, syngo.CT Coronary Cockpit
items.tldr: Siemens Healthineers won FDA clearance for software that uses AI to measure and map plaque across the coronary arteries on CT angiography scans.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Siemens Healthineers received US FDA clearance for syngo.CT Coronary Cockpit. The software runs inside the company's syngo.via imaging platform. It analyzes coronary CT angiography scans to quantify plaque in the heart arteries. The report came out on November 19, 2026, just ahead of the RSNA radiology meeting.

## Why it matters
Plaque analysis on coronary CT is moving from research into routine care. Measuring plaque by hand is slow and varies between readers. An automated tool from a major scanner vendor could make plaque metrics a standard part of reports. That matters for anyone building or validating coronary segmentation models, because it raises the bar for clinical-grade output.

## How it works
- AI segments the coronary tree, labels each artery and builds visualizations.
- It reports plaque amount, composition, size and distribution.
- Clinicians can review the whole tree or zoom into single lesions.
- The output supports choosing between stenting (PCI) and medicine, and helps plan PCI.
- It accepts CT angiography from any CT scanner. Siemens says it works best with its dual-source and photon-counting scanners.
- Siemens claims that coronary CT on its Naeotom Alpha photon-counting scanner can cut referrals for invasive diagnostic angiography by more than 50%, citing two studies in Radiology journals.

## Caveats
The article does not name the regulatory pathway, the clearance number or the exact indications for use. It gives no accuracy data for the plaque measurements. The 50% referral claim is a company statement tied to its own scanner, and the article gives no study sizes. Plaque values may not match between vendors, so numbers from different tools should not be mixed.

## Key terms
- **Coronary CT angiography (CCTA):** a CT scan with contrast dye that images the heart arteries.
- **Plaque composition:** the mix of calcified and non-calcified (softer, often riskier) material in an artery wall.
- **Segmentation:** outlining structures in an image, here the arteries and plaque, pixel by pixel.
- **Photon-counting CT:** a newer CT detector that counts individual X-ray photons for sharper, lower-noise images.
- **FDA clearance:** US permission to market a device, usually by showing it is similar to one already sold.

items.title: West Virginia University Health System picks Waystar's AI platform for its whole revenue cycle
items.tldr: A 31-hospital US health system will replace more than a dozen billing vendors with one AI-driven payment platform, aiming to cut claim denials and get paid faster.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
WVU Medicine, the West Virginia University Health System, chose Waystar to run its revenue cycle on a single software platform. The system has 31 hospitals across West Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Maryland. It employs more than 47,000 people and has about $10 billion in operating revenue. It plans to fold more than a dozen separate revenue cycle vendors into Waystar at first. Waystar calls this its largest new client by deal size, but gave no dollar figure.

## Why it matters
Billing is one of the most expensive back-office jobs in US hospitals. Each step, from checking a patient's insurance to appealing a rejected claim, often runs on a different tool. Data gets re-entered, errors creep in, and money leaks out. Consolidating vendors is a common way health systems try to make AI useful at scale: one data stream is easier to automate than twelve.

## Key details
- The platform uses Waystar's AI layer, branded AltitudeAI.
- It covers four stages: financial clearance (confirming coverage and cost before care), clinical integrity and revenue capture (making sure documented care is billed), claim management, and denial recovery.
- Goals named in the release: fewer denials, faster reimbursement, less manual work and less revenue leakage.
- The health system expects "millions" in extra reimbursement, with no specific number.
- Waystar says it handles 8.5 billion payment transactions and over $3 trillion in gross claims each year.

## Caveats
This is a vendor press release. It gives no baseline denial rate, no savings target and no go-live date. The word "initially" suggests a phased rollout with an unstated timeline. Claims about AI benefits are not yet backed by outcome data from this deployment. Readers should watch for later reports of real denial and cash-flow changes.

## Key terms
- **Revenue cycle**: every administrative step from scheduling and insurance checks to final payment for a patient's care.
- **Claim denial**: when an insurer refuses to pay a submitted bill, often for coding or paperwork errors.
- **Financial clearance**: confirming insurance coverage, prior approvals and patient cost before a visit.
- **Revenue leakage**: money a hospital earned but never collected, due to missed charges or unappealed denials.
- **Vendor consolidation**: replacing many separate software suppliers with one platform.

items.title: Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination for Hospital Patient Flow Optimization
items.tldr: In a simulation built from real hospital data, AI agents for each department that coordinated discharges and admissions cut total patient waiting time far below standard planning methods.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers at Kyoto University built an AI system that coordinates patient movement between hospital departments. Each department, such as the emergency department (ED), intensive care unit (ICU) or general medicine ward, gets its own AI agent. The agents learn when to speed up discharges and when to hold back new admissions. The team tested the system in a computer simulation built from real records of about 60,000 hospital admissions in the MIMIC-IV database.

## Why it matters
Bed flow is a daily crisis in many hospitals. A full ward backs up the ICU, which backs up the ED. Most planning tools assume steady demand and fixed routes. This paper instead mirrors how departments actually run: separately.

## How it works
The method uses multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several AI agents learn by trial and error to earn a shared reward. A queueing model of the hospital network acts as a built-in map of capacities and routes. Each agent sees five local signals, such as occupancy and queue length. It can raise discharge pace by up to 15% or gate admissions. Agents share summaries of their recent actions only with neighboring departments. A clinical mask blocks unsafe actions.

- Under a 25% demand surge, total patient delay fell to about 2,081 hours, versus 117,478 hours for a static model and 43,149 for a simple rule-based approach.
- Bounce-back transfers between wards fell to 1.7%, versus 7.4% in historical records.
- Removing cooperative routing raised delay to over 226,000 hours, so coordination did most of the work.

## Caveats
Everything happened in a simulator, not a real hospital. Service times come from historical averages and ignore staff fatigue and workload. The same model scored 2,081 hours in one table and 2,835 in another, which the authors attribute to different random seeds. Independent agents had fewer bounce-back transfers than the cooperative system. Only two safety measures were checked.

## Key terms
- **Patient flow**: how patients move from arrival through wards to discharge.
- **Reinforcement learning**: an AI method that learns actions by trial and error to maximize a reward.
- **Multi-agent system**: several AI agents, each controlling one part, learning to work together.
- **Queueing model**: math that describes waiting lines, arrival rates and service capacity.
- **MIMIC-IV**: a large, de-identified public database of US hospital and ICU records.

items.title: Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems
items.tldr: Doximity says more than 190 health systems now buy its AI scribe and clinical-question tools, while tighter hospital AI governance is reshaping who wins those contracts.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Doximity, a physician network and software company, reported quarterly results for the period ending September 30, 2026. It said more than 190 health systems have bought its AI suite, up from 165 the quarter before. Customers include 10 of the top 20 US hospitals. NewYork-Presbyterian has built Doximity's scribe and its clinical Q&A tool, Ask, into its electronic health record across 10 hospitals.

## Why it matters
Health systems are moving from scattered AI pilots to a few approved enterprise tools. Doximity's CEO said large systems are tightening AI governance around privacy, liability and security. That favors vendors with formal enterprise agreements. It also shows a business model tension: hospitals pay a "nominal" fee, while the company expects most money to come from pharma advertising.

## Key details
- About 900,000 of 1.8 million US prescribers used its workflow tools in the quarter; active users grew 34% year over year.
- A new patient context feature lets the AI read the chart, labs and history. UCSD Health is an early adopter. Prompts using it average 12 words, versus 24 without, because doctors no longer retype chart details.
- Doximity has privacy agreements with over 300 enterprise clients but has not finished AI reviews with all of them.
- It launched DoseCheck, a rule-based medication safety checker, and embeds UpToDate evidence content.
- Revenue was $174.5 million, up 4%. Net income fell to $34.7 million from $62.1 million as AI spending rose more than sixfold.

## Caveats
Usage and adoption figures are company-reported and not independently checked. The article gives no data on scribe note accuracy or clinician time saved. The ad-funded model raises questions about pharma influence near clinical decisions. Shares fell after the report on margin concerns.

## Key terms
- **Electronic health record (EHR)**: the hospital's digital patient chart system.
- **AI governance**: a health system's rules and review process for approving and monitoring AI tools.
- **Enterprise agreement**: an organization-wide contract, as opposed to individual doctors signing up.
- **Deterministic verifier**: a rule-based checker that always gives the same answer for the same input, unlike a chatbot.

items.title: Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Causality Assessment (MARCA) of Individual Case Safety Reports in Pharmacovigilance
items.tldr: A team of four cooperating AI agents scored whether a drug caused a reported side effect and matched expert pharmacovigilance reviewers on about 79% of drug-event pairs.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers at the University of Copenhagen and the University of Bologna built MARCA, a multi-agent AI system for causality assessment of adverse drug reaction reports. They tested it on 215 individual case safety reports from the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), covering early 2025. Those reports held 1,562 drug-event combinations. Human experts scored the same cases to create a reference standard.

## Why it matters
Safety report volumes keep rising, and each case needs an expert to judge whether the drug likely caused the event. That work is slow and hard to scale. Regulators and companies are exploring AI to triage cases. This study tests a structured, auditable approach rather than one general chatbot.

## How it works
MARCA follows the Naranjo scale, a 10-question checklist that rates how likely a drug caused a reaction. Four agents split the work. One searches PubMed for mechanism and evidence. One checks whether the event appears on the drug label. One decides whether the event is an objective sign or a subjective symptom. One combines everything into a causality report. The agents run on Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2. For some questions, the system retrieves similar expert-scored cases (retrieval-augmented generation) to guide its answer.

- Final causality category matched experts in 79.4% of combinations (kappa 0.587, moderate agreement).
- Question-level agreement ranged from 85.4% to 96.8%.
- In a 60-pair test, adding retrieval raised agreement on one question from 18.3% to 100%.

## Caveats
The authors list many limits. Data came from one database. One case alone contributed 371 combinations, and pairs within a case are not independent. The retrieval library overlapped with the test cases, which can inflate results. The 60-pair retrieval test was chosen from cases the system had already got wrong. Only one model pairing was tried. High percent agreement on some questions came with low kappa, meaning much of the match may be chance.

## Key terms
- **Pharmacovigilance**: monitoring drugs after approval to detect and assess side effects.
- **Individual case safety report (ICSR)**: a single report of a suspected drug side effect in one patient.
- **Naranjo scale**: a 10-question score classifying a reaction as definite, probable, possible or doubtful.
- **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**: the AI looks up relevant reference examples before answering.
- **Cohen's kappa**: an agreement score that corrects for chance; 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level.

items.title: EMA Quality Innovation Group roundtable on digitalisation and AI in pharmaceutical manufacturing
items.tldr: The EU drug regulator held a two-day public roundtable on how machine learning, digital twins and automation are being used in drug manufacturing and quality control.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) held an online roundtable on 18 and 19 November 2026. Its Quality Innovation Group (QIG) ran the meeting. The topic was digital and AI-enabled technology in pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality management. Industry, academics and regulators were invited to present real case studies. Both days were broadcast live, and an agenda was posted on 12 November.

## Why it matters
Manufacturing is where AI meets Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP), the strict rules that keep every batch of medicine safe and consistent. Regulators need to understand tools before they can write workable rules for them. EU GMP rules for AI are still being drafted, so meetings like this shape what inspectors will expect. For anyone building AI for quality control, this is an early view of regulator thinking.

## Key details
- Technologies named: data analytics, automation, machine learning and digital twins.
- Stated aims: share practical experience, explore scientific and regulatory challenges, and help QIG give timely regulatory support.
- Expected benefits listed: product quality, manufacturing efficiency, supply chain resilience and better decisions across a product's life.
- It follows two earlier QIG listen-and-learn meetings: on digital technologies in manufacturing and testing (12 October 2023) and on process models (4-5 June 2024).
- The meeting format is information exchange, not a formal consultation.

## Caveats
This is an event page, not binding guidance. It reports no outcomes, minutes or conclusions yet. The page does not say whether the draft EU GMP Annex 22 on AI was discussed. Any regulatory views shared at such meetings are not official positions until published as guidance.

## Key terms
- **Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)**: legal quality standards for how medicines are made and tested.
- **Quality Innovation Group (QIG)**: an EMA team that supports new technologies in medicine manufacturing and quality.
- **Digital twin**: a computer model of a real production process, updated with live data to predict its behavior.
- **Quality control**: testing raw materials and products to confirm they meet specifications.

items.title: EU GMP Annex 22 on AI: status of the draft after 1,359 consultation comments
items.tldr: Europe's proposed rules for AI in drug manufacturing drew 1,359 comments and may be widened to cover generative and adaptive models, but no final date is set.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A GMP consultancy published an updated status report on Annex 22, the EU's planned GMP chapter on artificial intelligence. The European Commission released the draft for consultation in July 2025, and comments closed in October 2025. The update, dated 13 November 2026, tracks what has happened since.

## Why it matters
Annex 22 will be the first EU rule written specifically for AI in medicine manufacturing. It decides which AI models drugmakers may use in critical steps, and how they must prove those models work. The original draft barred generative AI and large language models from critical uses. A change there would shift what companies can deploy on the factory floor.

## Key details
- The draft drew 1,359 comments from 79 organizations in 39 countries.
- Inspectors reviewed the comments in April 2026. A main theme was a risk-based approach without blanket technology bans.
- An expert workshop ran on 30 June and 1 July 2026. EMA published its report in early October 2026.
- The drafting group has discussed widening scope to dynamic, adaptive, probabilistic and generative models.
- The current draft allows only static, deterministic models in critical applications. Acceptance criteria must be set before testing and be at least as good as the process being replaced. Test data must be kept separate from development data. Drift monitoring is required in operation.
- No date is set for a revised draft or final text. Annex 11 on computerised systems still applies.

## Caveats
This is a consultancy summary, not an official EMA or Commission document. Scope changes are under discussion, not decided. Companies should check primary sources before changing validation plans. Timelines could slip further.

## Key terms
- **Annex 22**: a proposed EU GMP chapter setting rules for AI models used in medicine manufacturing.
- **Annex 11**: the existing EU GMP chapter on computerised systems.
- **Static, deterministic model**: an AI that does not change after release and gives the same output for the same input.
- **Model drift**: a fall in AI performance over time as real-world data changes.
- **Critical application**: a use that directly affects patient safety, product quality or data integrity.

items.title: Australia tightens its clinical decision support software exemption from 1 November 2026
items.source: Pure Global (summary of TGA instrument F2026L01167)
items.tldr: Australia's regulator rewrote the rules for which decision-support software can skip device registration, adding a ban on making diagnoses and a duty to show its reasoning.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) amended the exemption that lets some clinical decision support software (CDSS) avoid registration as a medical device. The change comes through legislative instrument F2026L01167, made on 3 September 2026. It took effect on 1 November 2026, with no transition period for CDSS.

## Why it matters
Many AI tools for clinicians sit near the line between helpful software and a regulated device. Rules like this decide whether a developer needs a full device listing. Australia's wording now closely tracks the US FDA approach, which asks that clinicians can check the software's basis. Developers selling in several markets need to watch for these shifts.

## Key details
The exemption now has five conditions that must all be met:
- The software makes a recommendation to a health professional to help a decision.
- Image or signal processing limits now also cover compression and decompression.
- It must not replace clinical judgement (unchanged in substance).
- New: it must not make a clinical diagnosis or treatment decision, including as diagnostic lab software.
- New: it must display the guidelines, calculations or logic behind each recommendation, so a professional can verify it.
Reporting duties stay the same. Serious public-health threats must be reported within 48 hours, and deaths or serious deterioration within 10 days. The rule covers devices made on or after 1 November, plus older stock used after that date.

## Caveats
The TGA says the update clarifies, rather than widens or narrows, the exemption. Others read the new conditions as stricter in practice. This summary comes from a regulatory consultancy, not the TGA itself. It notes the TGA's guidance lists 30 working days for supply notification, while the instrument says 20. Meeting the exemption does not remove all TGA oversight.

## Key terms
- **CDSS (clinical decision support software):** software that gives clinicians recommendations, such as alerts or risk scores.
- **Exemption:** a legal carve-out that lets a product skip some registration steps.
- **TGA:** Australia's regulator for medicines and medical devices.
- **ARTG:** the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, the official list of approved products.
- **Legislative instrument:** a binding regulation issued under an existing law.

items.title: EU AI Act delay for AI medical devices: what the Digital Omnibus changes
items.tldr: The EU pushed AI Act high-risk obligations for AI medical devices back to 2 August 2028, but the devices stay classed as high-risk and the requirements themselves are unchanged.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
The EU adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, called the Digital Omnibus on AI. It entered into force on 27 July 2026. It delays when the AI Act's high-risk rules apply to AI built into products such as medical devices and in vitro diagnostics (IVDs). Regulatory consultancy Cosm updated its explainer in November 2026 with corrections on the details.

## Why it matters
AI-enabled devices in the EU must meet both the medical device rules (MDR or IVDR) and the AI Act. Manufacturers now have a year more to prepare. But the work does not go away, so roadmaps should not stop. Anyone planning a CE-marked cardiac AI product needs the new dates.

## Key details
- High-risk duties for AI in medical devices and IVDs move from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028.
- Stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III move from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027.
- The Commission must adopt delegated acts by 2 August 2027 to remove duplication where MDR or IVDR already protect as well or better.
- AI medical devices remain high-risk systems. The required controls, including data governance, logging, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity, are unchanged.
- One notified-body assessment covering both laws is still the expected route.
- EN 18286, a quality-management standard for the AI Act, was approved in July 2026 and referenced in the Official Journal in October 2026.
- Parliament approved the package 423 to 57, with 174 abstentions.

## Caveats
A separate December 2025 Commission proposal to reform the MDR and IVDR could still change how the AI Act applies to devices. That proposal is still being negotiated. The practical burden will depend on the delegated acts and on standards that are not yet finished. Cosm is a consultancy, and its piece is analysis, not legal advice.

## Key terms
- **EU AI Act:** the EU law that sets risk-based rules for AI systems.
- **MDR / IVDR:** EU regulations for medical devices and for in vitro diagnostic tests.
- **High-risk AI system:** an AI Act category with the strictest duties, including most AI medical devices.
- **Notified body:** an independent organization the EU authorizes to certify devices.
- **Delegated act:** a rule the European Commission adopts to fill in details of a law.

items.title: Wellysis gets FDA 510(k) clearance for S-Patch CardioAI ECG analysis software
items.tldr: A Samsung spin-off won US clearance for stand-alone AI software that reads ECGs from its wearable patch and flags heart rhythm problems.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Wellysis, a 2019 spin-off from Samsung SDS, announced FDA 510(k) clearance for S-Patch CardioAI. The FDA cleared the product on 25 September 2026, and the company announced it on 8 October. It is software as a medical device (SaMD) in Class II. It analyzes ECG recordings and evaluates arrhythmias.

## Why it matters
The clearance covers the AI software separately from the patch hardware, which was already cleared. That split lets the company sell the algorithm on its own and embed it in other firms' apps. It shows a common regulatory pattern: clear the sensor first, then the analysis layer. Remote monitoring companies and diagnostic testing facilities are the target buyers.

## How it works
- The S-Patch is a wearable ECG sensor stuck to the chest.
- CardioAI takes the ECG data and automates rhythm analysis to support clinicians reading the tracing.
- It can be built into third-party web and mobile apps, with configurable analysis settings.
- The company plans subscription and per-test pricing.
- The patch also holds approval in Korea and a CE mark in Europe.

## Caveats
The release gives no accuracy figures, such as sensitivity or specificity. It does not list which arrhythmias are covered or give the 510(k) number. Without the FDA decision summary, readers cannot judge how well it performs or what predicate device it was compared to. Claims of growing US revenue come without dollar amounts. Check the FDA database entry before relying on the indications.

## Key terms
- **510(k):** an FDA pathway where a device is cleared by showing it is substantially equivalent to one already on the market.
- **SaMD (software as a medical device):** software that performs a medical purpose on its own, without being part of hardware.
- **Class II:** a moderate-risk US device category that needs specific controls and usually a 510(k).
- **Arrhythmia:** an abnormal heart rhythm, such as atrial fibrillation.
- **Predicate device:** the already-marketed device a new product is compared against in a 510(k).
